findings.headline: Council explicitly acknowledges limited resources prevent timely risk identification and management.
findings.detail: Section 9.1 states: 'Limited resource to ensure timely compliance with the processes in the RMS leaves the council unable to appropriately identify and manage a potentially significant wide range of risks.' The report flags this could lead to 'governance and service or project delivery failures' with 'profound' impacts 'in financial and health and wellbeing terms'.
findings.matters: A council that admits it cannot resource its own risk management processes may miss material financial or operational risks. This is a direct statement of governance capacity weakness.
findings.figures: None quantified; risk characterised as 'potentially significant wide range'
findings.quote: Limited resource to ensure timely compliance with the processes in the RMS leaves the council unable to appropriately identify and manage a potentially significant wide range of risks.

findings.headline: Corporate Risk Register data is over 6 months old, presented as current in Q4 report.
findings.detail: The report states the Corporate Risk Register is current 'as at the last run on 19 December 2025' but is being presented to committee on 29 June 2026. For a Q4 2025-26 report (covering to end March 2026), six-month-old risk data is stale and suggests the council may not be maintaining current visibility of its risks.
findings.matters: Risk registers are meant to be current. Stale data in a report to the audit committee indicates the council either has resource constraints or poor governance discipline in maintaining its risk framework.
findings.figures: Last run 19 December 2025; report presented 29 June 2026 (6+ month gap)
findings.quote: Appendix B shows the status as at the last run on 19 December 2025.

findings.headline: Risk report contains contradictory findings: opening recommendations claim no risk increases and no new risks; Section 3 later states 1 risk increase and 2 new risks.
findings.detail: The report's initial recommendations state 'NO risk level increases' and 'NO new risks added'. However, Section 3 of the same report contradicts this, stating 'there has been 1 risk level increase to either a Medium D or a High E' and 'There are 2 new risks'. The actual details of these risks are promised in appendices not provided in this extract. This inconsistency suggests either poor document control or a failure to reconcile updated information across the report.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's actual risk position. Internal contradictions in governance reporting suggest weak controls and raise questions about whether the council knows its true risk status.
findings.figures: 1 risk level increase; 2 new risks (details withheld in appendices)
findings.quote: Initial recommendation: 'Notes that there has been NO risk level increases' vs. Section 3.2: 'That Members note that there has been 1 risk level increase to either a Medium D or a High E'

findings.headline: Treasury operations generated £0.231m net interest income despite the new £8m borrowing, outperforming expectations
findings.detail: The council managed its cash to generate returns while funding capital investment. Although it anticipated that net interest costs would be required in 2025/26, it actually achieved net interest income of £0.231m at an average portfolio return of 3.71%. The Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream improved from -2.29% to -0.98%, both negative figures indicating net interest income rather than cost.
findings.matters: Shows the council has active, competent treasury management that generated positive returns while funding capital needs, enhancing the council's financial position despite taking on new debt.
findings.figures: Interest income £0.231m; average investment return 3.71%; average investment size £1.647m; Financing Costs ratio -0.98%
findings.quote: No target was set for 2025/26 as it was assumed that a net interest payable amount would be required to meet the Council's capital programme. Actual interest income from interest activity amounted to £0.231m.

findings.headline: Council took on £8m new debt in 2025/26, shifting from a net cash position to net borrowing
findings.detail: The council had zero external debt at the end of 2024/25 but borrowed £8m during 2025/26 at an average rate of 5.4%. This borrowing was within the approved Operational Boundary of £80m and represented the first time the council has used external borrowing in recent years.
findings.matters: A material change in the council's debt position is a significant financial decision that a lender would need to understand in terms of the council's capital programme, debt sustainability, and capacity to service new obligations.
findings.figures: Total Debt increased from £0 (2024/25) to £8m (2025/26); average rate 5.4%; Operational Boundary £80m; used 10% of limit

findings.headline: Regeneration scheme contract management was not operational at audit time; now being monitored with independent quantity surveyor
findings.detail: Ryecroft, Midway Car Park and Astley Place regeneration schemes had planned but not yet operational client-side contract management at audit time. High priority recommendation raised. Now arrangements in place using check/challenge meetings, formal progress meetings, draw down schedules, and independent quantity surveyor to value and certify works against contract value.
findings.matters: Capital schemes with weak initial governance pose risk of overspend or developer non-performance; follow-up assurance has been added to 2026-27 plan
findings.figures: One high priority recommendation; three schemes affected (Ryecroft, Midway Car Park, Astley Place)
findings.quote: Client-side contract management arrangements for the Ryecroft, Midway Car Park and Astley Place regeneration schemes was made. At the time of audit, key arrangements for oversight of the build phase were planned but not yet operational.

findings.headline: No formal approval process for homelessness service credit card spending; historically given verbally only
findings.detail: High priority finding on Homelessness and Rough Sleepers Grants: credit card expenditure was approved verbally with no documented audit trail. No assurance that purchases were appropriate, authorised, or linked to assessed client need. Now documented formal approval process in place with transactions reviewed before or after spend.
findings.matters: Absence of documented approval for public spending weakens assurance on proper use of funds; risk of improper expenditure was present
findings.figures: One high priority recommendation; now implemented
findings.quote: A high priority recommendation was raised as no formal process was in place for approving credit card expenditure, with approvals given verbally and no documented audit trail retained. This weakened assurance that purchases were appropriate, authorised and linked to assessed client need, increasing the risk of improper use of public funds.

findings.headline: Multiple financial systems lack documented policies and rely on manual processes without independent review
findings.detail: Recurring theme across E-Payments, Accounts Receivable, and others: key processes not clearly documented, policies not reviewed recently (Accounts Receivable policy not updated since 2023), manual reconciliations performed without independent review, and insufficient audit trails. E-Payments and Main Accounting both have manual reconciliations with no independent check.
findings.matters: Undocumented and manual processes are prone to error and harder to audit; lack of independent review means errors or fraud could persist
findings.figures: Multiple systems in draft or with Adequate Assurance; Accounts Receivable policy last reviewed 2023
findings.quote: In a number of areas, arrangements were operating in practice but were not fully documented, formally approved, version controlled or kept up to date.

findings.headline: Capacity and resourcing pressures explicitly constraining control effectiveness across multiple functions
findings.detail: The audit identifies capacity and resourcing as a cross-cutting theme affecting control consistency. Accounts Receivable reconciliations were not completed for a period due to resourcing pressures. Supported Accommodation implementation was delayed due to capacity. Audit staff turnover meant audits were reallocated and delayed; Service Director for Legal and Governance departure caused further delays.
findings.matters: A council facing sustained capacity constraints cannot reliably operate its financial controls; this is a structural risk rather than a single fixable issue
findings.figures: Audit work 'indicated' capacity pressures in 'some areas'; two audits not completed due to staff turnover and timing; Senior Audit Manager directing work through service agreement with Staffordshire County Council (341 days delivered)
findings.quote: Audit work also indicated that, in some areas, capacity and resourcing pressures were affecting the consistency with which controls could be operated or followed through in practice.

findings.headline: Debt recovery is not progressing in timely manner with delays in enforcement and prolonged case inactivity
findings.detail: Accounts Receivable audit found debt recovery activity delayed with inadequate escalation and enforcement. Cases remain inactive for extended periods and debts are not being advanced to appropriate enforcement stages. Management is implementing automated scheduling of recovery action, but the audit found limited visibility due to reliance on manual spreadsheets with no independent review.
findings.matters: Slow debt recovery directly affects cash collection and council liquidity; weak oversight means money owed is not being pursued effectively
findings.figures: Accounts Receivable given Adequate Assurance (Draft); one high priority recommendation on debt recovery process
findings.quote: Debt recovery activity is not being progressed in a timely and controlled manner, with delays in reminder and escalation actions, prolonged inactivity on cases, and debts not being advanced to appropriate enforcement stages where recovery remains outstanding.

findings.headline: Payroll control weaknesses including shared admin accounts and users approving their own changes
findings.detail: The payroll audit resulted in Limited Assurance due to three high priority issues: shared administrator accounts used by multiple officers (preventing attribution of actions), lack of prompt access removal when staff leave relevant roles, and inadequate segregation of duties allowing users to submit and approve their own payroll amendments including changes to their own records. Management is liaising with Stoke-on-Trent City Council (payroll provider) to issue individual accounts.
findings.matters: Weak controls over payroll processing create fraud risk and reduce accountability; the council cannot currently audit who made what change to payroll records
findings.figures: Three high priority recommendations; one additional security-related recommendation withheld
findings.quote: Collectively, these weaknesses increased the risk of unauthorised or inappropriate changes to payroll records, fraud, error and reduced accountability, and were a key factor in the limited assurance opinion for this review.

findings.headline: The council is planning a £110.010m capital programme for 2026/27 to 2028/29, financed significantly by borrowing.
findings.detail: The capital programme includes major investment in regeneration schemes via Town Deals funding, but also requires substantial borrowing. The Capital Financing Requirement will increase to £31.279m by 2027/28. Of the £145.645m total funding across four years, £56.893m is regeneration borrowing, indicating new debt taken on for capital projects.
findings.matters: This represents significant new borrowing that increases the council's debt servicing costs and financial risk if tax base growth or capital receipts do not materialise as expected.
findings.figures: £110.010m capital programme (2026-2029); CFR rising to £31.279m by 2027/28; £56.893m regeneration borrowing out of £145.645m total funding
findings.quote: The proposed Capital Programme for 2026/27 to 2028/29 is based on new schemes which are vital to ensure continued service delivery and in assisting the Council to achieve its corporate and service objectives as set out in the Council Plan 2022-26. These schemes total £110.010m including major investment into the Borough via external funding in terms of the Town Deals Fund for both Newcastle and Kidsgrove and associated projects.

findings.headline: The council is absorbing £0.233m of employer National Insurance costs in 2026/27 without government compensation.
findings.detail: In 2025/26, changes to NI contribution rates created a £0.403m pressure. The government reimbursed only £0.170m, leaving the council to absorb £0.233m. This uncompensated cost is built into the 2026/27 budget.
findings.matters: This demonstrates that government is not fully compensating councils for policy-driven cost increases, reducing financial flexibility and creating ongoing pressure on operational budgets.
findings.figures: £0.403m total pressure; £0.170m government reimbursement; £0.233m uncompensated
findings.quote: Changes to Employers National Insurance Contribution rates and the associated thresholds for 2025/26 amounted to a pressure of £0.403m, it was confirmed on 3 February 2025 that only £0.170m of this will be reimbursed by Central Government, as such a pressure of £0.233m for 2026/27 has been recognised.

findings.headline: The Budget Support Fund for Homelessness is declining year-on-year from £324k to £102k across three years.
findings.detail: The homelessness support reserve is being drawn down from £324k (31.3.25) to £152k (31.3.26) to £102k (31.3.27), losing 68% of its value. This reserve is specifically held to manage homelessness costs and its depletion suggests rising demand exceeding budget support.
findings.matters: Combined with the temporary accommodation pressure above, this shows sustained homelessness demand that is consuming reserves and may require continued budget supplementation or service cuts.
findings.quote: Budget Support Fund (Homelessness): Balance 31.3.25 £324k; Forecast Balance 31.3.26 £152k; Forecast Balance 31.3.27 £102k

findings.headline: The Business Rates reserve is being drawn down by £761k to cover collection deficits from 2024/25 and 2025/26.
findings.detail: The Business Rates reserve forecast shows a decline from £2,675k at 31 March 2026 to £1,914k at 31 March 2027. This is explicitly stated as covering repayment of collection deficits. This reduces a key financial buffer and signals ongoing business rates collection risk.
findings.matters: Depletion of the business rates reserve to cover collection deficits reduces the council's shock absorber and suggests underlying weakness in business rates income stability.
findings.figures: Reserve balance falling from £2,675k to £1,914k (£761k reduction); Business Rates reserve down from £1,363k (31.3.25) to £2,675k (31.3.26) to £1,914k (31.3.27)
findings.quote: A deficit relating to 2024/25 and 2025/26 will be repayable by the Council in 2026/27 – the reduced forecast balance at 31 March 2027 of the reserve reflects this repayment.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs are rising; the council is budgeting an additional £0.194m for 2026/27.
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation is a demand-led service where the council has had to build in specific cost pressure. This is linked to the documented issue that housing building has not kept up with demand, creating an affordability gap and pressure on homelessness services.
findings.matters: Rising temporary accommodation costs indicate increasing homelessness pressure in the borough, which is a direct demand-driven cost that is difficult to control and may exceed budget.
findings.figures: £0.194m pressure in 2026/27
findings.quote: A small number of new pressures facing the Council in 2026/27 have also been provided for, these include an allowance for costs associated with Local Government Re-organisation amounting to £0.400m (decreasing to £0.200m in 2027/28 and nil in 2028/29) and temporary accommodation demands (£0.194m).

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will cost the council £0.400m in 2026/27 and £0.200m in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The MTFS explicitly budgets for costs associated with Local Government Reorganisation starting immediately, indicating the council is preparing for sector restructuring or merger. This is a one-off pressure that then disappears from 2028/29 onwards.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand the operational and financial implications of anticipated local government restructuring, which could affect service continuity and debt management.
findings.quote: A small number of new pressures facing the Council in 2026/27 have also been provided for, these include an allowance for costs associated with Local Government Re-organisation amounting to £0.400m (decreasing to £0.200m in 2027/28 and nil in 2028/29) and temporary accommodation demands (£0.194m).

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will redistribute £0.126m of funding away from the council in 2026/27, with further reductions of £0.454m and £0.472m in following years.
findings.detail: The council received £9.360m in 2025/26 subject to redistribution under the Fair Funding Review 2.0. This reduces to £9.234m in 2026/27 and continues falling in subsequent years. A £0.500m reserve was set aside to cover these reductions, but this only partially offsets the multi-year hit.
findings.matters: This represents a structural loss of government funding that the council cannot recover and reduces financial flexibility to absorb other pressures.
findings.figures: £0.126m loss in 2026/27, £0.454m in 2027/28, £0.472m in 2028/29; funding reducing from £9.360m to £9.234m
findings.quote: Funding received and retained by the Council in 2025/26 that is subject to redistribution under the Fair Funding Review amounts to £9.360m, including the benefits referred to at 2.17, for 2026/27 this will amount to £9.234m – a reduction in funding of £0.126m. With further reductions of £0.454m in 2027/28 and £0.472m in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budgets and Strategies 2026-27, FEBRUARY 2026 - Council
findings.headline: Future budget stability dependent on non-recurring funding sources: Recovery Grant (£398-500k) and Extended Producer Responsibility (£274k).
findings.detail: The council is using Recovery Grant funding of £398k in 2027/28 and £500k in 2028/29 to offset settlement reductions, explicitly to 'smooth the impact of the Fair Funding Review 2.0'. Additionally, Extended Producer Responsibility income (£274k) is being used to fund 2026/27 savings. Neither source is permanent government funding, and the Recovery Grant is explicitly temporary smoothing of a structural funding cliff.
findings.matters: Using temporary grants and non-base revenue to plug structural deficits defers but does not solve underlying financial problems. When Recovery Grant expires after 2028/29, the council will face further unbudgeted gaps unless additional permanent savings are identified, suggesting the 2030/31 funding gap may be understated.
findings.figures: Recovery Grant 2027/28: £398k, 2028/29: £500k (both identified as temporary smoothing); Extended Producer Responsibility 2026/27: £274k
findings.quote: The increase in the minimum level will be financed from the Recovery Grant to be received in 2026/27, the balance of which will be paid into the Budget and Borrowing Support Fund to increase the Council's financial resilience, ahead of its use in 2027/28 and 2028/29 to smooth the impact of the Fair Funding Review 2.0.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budgets and Strategies 2026-27, FEBRUARY 2026 - Council
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing to £31.279m by 2028/29 dependent on three regeneration projects delivering forecast capital receipts.
findings.detail: The council is pursuing a £110m capital programme over 2026/27-2028/29, with Capital Financing Requirement growing 57% from £19.893m (March 2025) to £31.279m (March 2029). Three major schemes—York Place (£13.451m), Midway Carpark (£32.237m), and Ryecroft (£29.078m)—dominate the programme. Crucially, interest is being capitalised on these schemes based on assumptions they will generate capital receipts. Slippage or underperformance in receipt realisations would increase revenue debt servicing costs.
findings.matters: A lender tracks debt trajectory and the assumptions underlying capital strategies. Betting on capital receipts from three concurrent regeneration schemes that have not yet delivered creates execution risk. Failed or delayed receipts would force revenue budget to absorb capitalised interest costs.
findings.figures: CFR at 31/3/25: £19.893m; forecast at 31/3/29: £31.279m (57% growth); York Place capitalised interest, Midway capitalised interest, Ryecroft capitalised interest all dependent on receipt realisation
findings.quote: The Capital Programme for 2026/27 to 2028/29 includes an estimate for the development of York Place, which has been updated to reflect an adjusted cashflow and receipt of Homes England funding (£5.076m), this assumes spend of £13.451m plus capitalised interest over the period 2026/27 to 2027/28 and a subsequent capital receipt including capitalised interest during 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budgets and Strategies 2026-27, FEBRUARY 2026 - Council
findings.headline: Unresolved funding gaps in MTFS beyond 2026/27, with 2030/31 showing £365k residual gap after all identified savings.
findings.detail: While 2026/27 budget is balanced, the 5-year MTFS shows only partial solutions to future deficits. After savings of £560k are applied in 2030/31, a gap of £365k remains unfunded. Additionally, potential loss of recycling credits (£195k in 2027/28, £250k in 2028/29) if the County Council takes contractor disposal is flagged as a material risk.
findings.matters: A residual funding gap in the final year of the MTFS indicates either the savings plan is incomplete or further service reductions will be needed. Lenders assess councils on whether they have credible multi-year financial plans; unresolved deficits in the outer years are a warning sign.
findings.figures: 2030/31 remaining gap £365k after £560k identified savings; potential recycling income loss £195k (2027/28) and £250k (2028/29)
findings.quote: The MTFS indicates a budget shortfall of £1.599m for 2026/27, further years funding gaps are shown on the table below and in further detail at Appendix 5.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budgets and Strategies 2026-27, FEBRUARY 2026 - Council
findings.headline: Household waste service forecast to overspend by £0.275m in 2025/26 due to agency staffing and contractor costs.
findings.detail: Overtime, casual and agency staffing within Household Waste and Food Waste Services, combined with increased contractor disposal payments, has created an overspend of £0.206m at quarter three, forecast to reach £0.275m for the full year. This represents a structural cost pressure in what should be a controlled statutory service.
findings.matters: Inability to control costs in a core statutory waste service through labour market pressures and contractor pricing suggests the council faces systemic cost inflation that may affect other services. Forecasting accuracy is also at risk if in-year variances are this large.
findings.figures: £0.206m actual at Q3, £0.275m forecast full year overspend
findings.quote: Use of overtime, casual and agency staff within the Household Waste and Food Waste Services along with increased contractor disposal payments has resulted in an overspend of £0.206m at the close of quarter three. It is forecast that this will amount to an overspend of £0.275m for the financial year.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budgets and Strategies 2026-27, FEBRUARY 2026 - Council
findings.headline: Business Rates Collection Fund deficit of £1.193m due to successful property appeals creating reserve drawdown.
findings.detail: The council faces a Business Rates Collection Fund deficit estimated at £2.982m across all preceptors for 2025/26, of which the council's share is £1.193m. This results from successful property appeals in January-March 2025, creating an adverse variance of £2.291m from the December 2024 forecast. The deficit will be covered by drawdown from Business Rates Reserve.
findings.matters: Material reserve drawdown to cover appeal-driven funding volatility demonstrates significant valuation risk in business rates income. Reserves are being depleted to manage volatility rather than accumulated as resilience buffer.
findings.figures: Collection fund deficit £2.982m (council share £1.193m); variance from forecast £2.291m adverse
findings.quote: The Business Rates Collection Fund is estimated to be in a deficit position at the close of 2025/26. The deficit is estimated to amount to £2.982m, of which the Council's share is £1.193m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue and Capital Budgets and Strategies 2026-27, FEBRUARY 2026 - Council
findings.headline: Multiple revenue streams underperforming in 2025/26, with income shortfalls forecast to continue affecting cashflow.
findings.detail: Car parking, bereavement services, leisure memberships (pool closure), trade waste and land charges are all recording income significantly below budget in quarter three 2025/26. These shortfalls are forecast to total £0.504m for the full year (excluding the pool closure which is £0.254m additional). This suggests structural rather than temporary weakness in discretionary income sources.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the stability of a council's cash-generating services. Simultaneous underperformance across multiple unrelated revenue streams (parking, leisure, bereavement, waste) suggests market weakness or demand issues, not one-off problems.
findings.figures: Car parking £0.137m, trade waste £0.075m, bereavement services £0.176m, pool closure £0.254m forecast full year impact
findings.quote: Income shortfalls at the close of quarter three from car parking (£0.137m), trade waste (£0.075m), land charges (£0.044m) and bereavement services (£0.176m). It is forecast that these will total £0.504m for the financial year.

findings.headline: Authorised borrowing limit being increased from £75m to £170m, more than doubling the legal ceiling on external debt
findings.detail: The council is seeking Full Council approval to increase the maximum permitted borrowing from £75m (2025/26) to £170m (2028/29). This 127% increase in four years signals a strategic shift from reserve-funded to debt-funded capital investment.
findings.matters: Doubling the authorised borrowing limit requires explicit Council approval and signals that the council intends to move substantially into debt financing; it indicates both need and increased financial risk appetite
findings.quote: The Council is asked to approve the following authorised limit: Debt 75,000 [2025/26] 120,000 [2026/27] 145,000 [2027/28] 170,000 [2028/29]

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing 57% over four years, from £19.9m to £31.3m by 2028/29
findings.detail: The CFR—the underlying borrowing need—will rise from £19.893m (31 March 2025) to £31.279m (31 March 2029). This substantial increase represents the council's structural reliance on debt to fund the capital programme.
findings.matters: A rising CFR signals increasing structural debt; prudential regulation requires it to remain below the authorised limit and lenders track this trend as a measure of financial stress
findings.quote: The Capital Financing Requirement is set to increase to £31.279m by 2028/29 based on the 3-year Capital Programme for 2026/27 to 2028/29, the Capital Financing Requirement at 31 March 2025 (£19.893m)

findings.headline: Borrowing costs rising to £2.1m/year by 2035/36, totalling £16.2m over ten years and consuming growing share of revenue budget
findings.detail: Minimum revenue provision and interest payments will cost the revenue budget £16.2m over ten years, rising from £1.04m in 2026/27 to £2.11m by 2035/36. The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream will rise from 4.80% to 6.33% by 2028/29, indicating increasing pressure on day-to-day spending.
findings.matters: Capital borrowing is not free; the council's revenue budget will bear increasing annual costs that reduce funds available for other services, and the trend worsens into the 2030s
findings.quote: The costs to the revenue budget relating to minimum revenue provision and interest payable on borrowings will be around £16.163m over 10 years, with the costs in each year 2026/27 to 2035/36 being as shown below

findings.headline: Regeneration projects worth £70m+ depend on asset sales from 2028/29 onwards that may not materialise on schedule
findings.detail: Regeneration spending peaks at £53.8m in 2026/27 and £23m in 2027/28, initially funded by 'regeneration borrowing.' The strategy assumes capital receipts will emerge from 2028/29 (£13.4m), 2029/30 (£27.3m), and 2030/31 (£32.7m) to service this debt. If asset sales fail or are delayed, the borrowing remains outstanding.
findings.matters: A material portion of the capital programme is predicated on disposing of regenerated assets within specific timescales; delayed sales extend the borrowing period and increase financing costs
findings.figures: Regeneration borrowing: £47.2m (2026/27), £23m (2027/28); Regeneration receipts expected: £13.4m (2028/29), £27.3m (2029/30), £32.7m (2030/31)
findings.quote: The Capital Programme will require to be financed by borrowing, primarily for cash flow purposes, whilst assets are procured and constructed, after which time significant capital receipts are expected.

findings.headline: £142.3m capital programme cannot be funded from capital receipts alone; significant borrowing is required
findings.detail: Over 2026/27 to 2035/36, capital expenditure totals £142.3m. The council explicitly states there will be insufficient receipts to meet all costs, creating a structural funding gap that must be met through borrowing across the entire decade.
findings.matters: Planned capital investment far exceeds available receipts, forcing the council into structural debt financing and reducing financial flexibility
findings.figures: £142.3m capital programme; £21.4m from capital receipts (15%); £11.5m from borrowing; remainder from external contributions and expected regeneration receipts
findings.quote: There will be insufficient capital receipts arising from planned sales to meet all the costs of the investment programme.

findings.headline: Right to Buy capital receipts have collapsed from a historically major funding source to £0.5m per annum
findings.detail: The council previously relied heavily on capital receipts from Aspire Housing Right to Buy sales. The strategy states these have 'diminished from historically high levels, both because of the present depressed property market and there being fewer potential purchasers as time goes by.' This substantially reduces the council's self-funding capacity for capital investment.
findings.matters: A major revenue stream that funded capital investment has effectively dried up, forcing reliance on borrowing and asset sales instead
findings.figures: Future Right to Buy sales income projected at £0.5m per annum
findings.quote: However, Right to Buy sales have diminished from historically high levels, both because of the present depressed property market and there being fewer potential purchasers as time goes by. Future sales income is projected to be in the range of £0.5m per annum.

findings.headline: Council holds £2.007m in general reserves specifically to cover investment property income shortfalls
findings.detail: The council has set aside this amount as a contingency against the possibility of net shortfalls from its commercial property investments. This reflects management's assessment that volatility in this revenue source is material enough to require dedicated reserve cover.
findings.matters: The size of the reserve relative to budget swing shows management views investment property income risk as material and real
findings.figures: £2.007m held in General Fund balances
findings.quote: A total of £2.007m is currently held in balances to cover this and other risks and can be drawn upon in the event of risks materialising.

findings.headline: Council's budget depends on returns from a commercial property portfolio that has made losses in three of the past four years
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it is dependent on commercial property rental income to achieve a balanced revenue budget. Yet the portfolio returned losses of £36k (2022/23), £142k (2023/24), and £93k (2024/25), before projecting a £122k profit for 2025/26. This shows material volatility in a revenue stream the council has declared essential.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's budget stability rests on a volatile asset class, and whether the recent recovery will hold
findings.figures: 2022/23 £36k loss, 2023/24 £142k loss, 2024/25 £93k loss, 2025/26 £122k profit (estimate), 2026/27 £125k profit (estimate)
findings.quote: The Council is dependent on a return from investment property activity in terms of rentals to achieve a balanced revenue budget.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing £7.4m (37%) over three years from capital programme that is not fully resourced
findings.detail: CFR rises from £19.9m (31 March 2025 actual) to £32.3m (31 March 2028 forecast), a 62% increase. The strategy notes the council 'may therefore be required to borrow over the forecast period' and that it 'expects to comply' with CIPFA's Prudential Code recommendation that total debt be lower than highest forecast CFR. The implication is that existing resources are insufficient and borrowing is necessary.
findings.matters: Growing CFR means the council's capital ambition is expanding faster than its internal resources can fund; understanding what is driving this capital spend is essential.
findings.quote: The Council has an increasing CFR due to the capital programme and may therefore be required to borrow over the forecast period.

findings.headline: Interest rate forecast depends on November 2025 Budget and assumes Bank Rate falls to 3.75%, but risks are both up and down
findings.detail: Arlingclose forecast (dated 10 November 2024) assumes Bank Rate reaching 3.75% and holding there through 2026-28. However, the strategy explicitly notes this was issued before the November 2025 Budget and 'is likely to be revised'. The forecast shows material downside risks (Bank Rate could fall to 2.75% or lower) but also upside risks to yields. The council's strategy to borrow short-term now and long-term later depends on long-term rates falling or at least not rising sharply.
findings.matters: If the Budget or subsequent economic data shift the interest rate outlook, the council's borrowing costs and refinancing plans could change materially.
findings.figures: Arlingclose central case: Bank Rate 3.75% (from Dec-25 through Sep-28); downside risk: -1.00% (Bank Rate could reach 2.75%); 10-yr gilt yield forecast 4.40% with downside risk of -1.10%; Debt interest budget 2026-27: £738,780
findings.quote: This forecast was issued ahead of the Autumn Budget and is likely to be revised once the fiscal measures are announced on 26th November 2025 and their market implications are assessed.

findings.headline: Council deferring external borrowing by drawing on reserves and internal resources rather than taking long-term debt now
findings.detail: The strategy is explicit: maintain internal borrowing (using reserves and cash) rather than external debt, switching to external long-term borrowing only when interest rates are favorable. Currently holding £8.93m invested while forecasting need to borrow. Usable reserves forecast to remain between £9.9m and £10.6m across the period, providing the buffer for this strategy.
findings.matters: This defers certainty of financing costs but creates refinancing risk if long-term rates don't fall as expected or if the council needs cash sooner than planned.
findings.figures: Treasury investments held: £8.93m (14 Jan 2026); Usable reserves: £10.6m (2026), £9.9m (2027), £10.0m (2028-2029); Budget for investment income 2026-27: nil
findings.quote: The Council's current strategy is to maintain borrowing and investments below their underlying levels, sometimes known as internal borrowing. Where borrowing is required, this will be in line with Arlingclose's current advice of doing so from other local authorities on a short-term basis. This will be undertaken until it becomes advantageous to switch to long term debt, with the lowest cost option being considered.

findings.headline: Borrowing strategy dependent on capital receipts from regeneration projects not arriving until 2028-29
findings.detail: The forecast assumes capital receipts will materialise from regeneration projects starting in 2028-29, after which net loans requirement is forecast to fall from £87.6m to £73.3m by 2029. The council is currently using internal resources (reserves and working capital) to delay external borrowing, but if regeneration receipts are delayed or fall short, the refinancing risk and debt burden could be substantially worse.
findings.matters: Regeneration projects are discretionary and timings are uncertain; a lender needs to know what happens to cash flow and debt if expected receipts don't materialise.
findings.figures: Forecast net loans requirement falls from £87.6m (2028) to £73.3m (2029), an assumption built on capital receipts 'expected from 2028/29 onwards'; current working capital forecast shows swing from negative £9.3m (2026) through positive £65.3m (2028) to positive £52.0m (2029)
findings.quote: borrowing relating to regeneration projects, for which capital receipts are expected from 2028/29 onwards

findings.headline: External borrowing forecast to escalate sharply from zero to £87.6m by 2028-29 driven by capital expansion
findings.detail: The council currently holds no external borrowing but the liability benchmark forecasts net loans requirement of £7.5m in 2026, jumping to £61.3m by 2027 and peaking at £87.6m by 2028. This represents a fundamental shift from the council's current position as a net investor (£8.93m held 14 January 2026) to substantial external borrowing. The underlying driver is the Capital Financing Requirement growing from £27.4m to £32.3m over the period.
findings.matters: A council moving from holding cash to taking on £87.6m of debt signals major capital commitments ahead, and a lender needs to understand both the projects being funded and the council's ability to service that debt.
findings.figures: External borrowing forecast: £7.5m (2026), £61.3m (2027), £87.6m (2028); CFR: £27.4m (2026), £29.0m (2027), £32.3m (2028); Current holdings: £0 external borrowing, £8.93m investments
findings.quote: The balance sheet forecasts, in the table above, shows that the Council expects to borrow in 2026/27, in addition to undertaking borrowing towards the backend of the current year.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Capital Budget 2026-27 - First Draft Savings Plans - DECEMBER 2025 - FAPS.doc
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer flags 'significant budget risks' and dependency on reserves to manage unforeseen pressures
findings.detail: The S151 officer's report acknowledges that budget risks — overspending, income shortfalls, and funding changes — are material in the context of Government funding reform uncertainty. The officer explicitly states that reserves must be sufficient to absorb unforeseen pressures. The robustness assessment is provisional and will only be confirmed in February 2026.
findings.matters: The council's own finance officer is flagging limited headroom and expecting to draw reserves; this signals constrained financial resilience
findings.figures: No specific reserve balances disclosed; robustness opinion provisional until February 2026 final budget
findings.quote: In the context of uncertainty regarding Government funding reforms there are significant budget risks that will need to be managed. It will be essential the Council has sufficient reserves to call on if required.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Capital Budget 2026-27 - First Draft Savings Plans - DECEMBER 2025 - FAPS.doc
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement will grow by £11.4m to £31.278m by 2028/29, increasing debt service burden
findings.detail: The council's CFR at March 2025 was £19.893m. With the three-year capital programme of £109.946m (including £56.565m of regeneration borrowing), the CFR is forecast to reach £31.278m by 2028/29. This represents an increase in debt principal and an ongoing increase in annual debt-servicing costs.
findings.matters: Growing CFR increases the council's debt service costs and reduces financial flexibility; debt servicing is an ongoing obligation that competes with service spending
findings.figures: CFR 31 March 2025: £19.893m, forecast CFR 31 March 2029: £31.278m, three-year capital spend £109.946m, regeneration borrowing £56.565m
findings.quote: The Capital Financing Requirement is set to increase to £31.278m by 2028/29 based on the 3 year Capital Programme for 2026/27 to 2028/29, the Capital Financing Requirement at 31 March 2025 (£19.893m) and the Capital Financing Requirement for capital expenditure during the current financial year and the financial years 2026/27 to 2028/29 (£11.385m).

findings.paper_title: Revenue Capital Budget 2026-27 - First Draft Savings Plans - DECEMBER 2025 - FAPS.doc
findings.headline: £88m of the £109.946m capital programme (80%) depends on unproven business cases for three regeneration schemes
findings.detail: Three major projects are included in the capital plan: York Place (£18.136m), Midway Carpark (£36.350m), and Aparthotel on Ryecroft (£33.712m). Each is explicitly marked 'subject to the business case that is currently being developed'. Together they represent £88m of planned spend. If any fail approval, the council has material borrowing exposure with no offsetting capital receipts to repay it.
findings.matters: Regeneration schemes deliver the capital receipts needed to fund the capital programme and pay down borrowing; if business cases fail, the council carries unplanned debt
findings.figures: York Place £18.136m, Midway Carpark £36.350m, Aparthotel £33.712m, total £88.198m of £109.946m three-year programme
findings.quote: The Capital Programme also includes an estimate for an Aparthotel on the Ryecroft site of £33.712m over the period 2025/26 to 2029/30 together with a subsequent capital receipt of the same value plus capitalised interest in 2030/31. Again, this is subject to the business case that is currently being developed.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Capital Budget 2026-27 - First Draft Savings Plans - DECEMBER 2025 - FAPS.doc
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will cut funding by £964k in 2026/27, a structural loss not fully resolved
findings.detail: The council receives £9.360m in 2025/26 from Business Rates Retention and grants subject to Fair Funding Review redistribution. This drops to £8.396m in 2026/27 — a £964k structural cut. The council set aside £500k in the prior year, leaving £464k of this loss unfunded in the budget gap. Recovery is not expected until 2028/29.
findings.matters: Structural funding losses of nearly £1m cannot be closed by one-off savings and require sustained service reductions or efficiency gains — a material ongoing pressure
findings.figures: £9.360m (2025/26) → £8.396m (2026/27), £964k loss, £464k gap remaining after prior-year provision
findings.quote: Funding received and Business Rates retained by the Council in 2025/26 that are subject to redistribution under the Fair Funding Review amount to £9.360m, for 2026/27 it is anticipated through comprehensive modelling that this will amount to £8.396m – a reduction in funding of £0.964m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Housing supply assumption of 3,718 properties over five years underpins council tax base growth, but borough has 'low levels of house building'
findings.detail: The MTFS assumes the housing market supply requirement of 3,718 properties over five years will be met per the trajectory in the draft Local Plan, thus increasing the tax base accordingly. However, the document notes that the borough has 'in recent decades it has seen low levels of house building which have not kept up with housing demand,' and this affordability gap is driving pressure on homelessness and temporary accommodation services.
findings.matters: If the draft Local Plan trajectory for house building is not met, council tax base growth assumptions fail, worsening future-year budget gaps. The affordability gap also signals demand pressure on services.
findings.figures: 3,718 properties assumed over 5-year period
findings.quote: Newcastle-under-Lyme has a growing population, but in recent decades it has seen low levels of house building which have not kept up with housing demand. The resulting affordability gap for residents influenced by the cost of living puts pressure on our homelessness and temporary accommodations services.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement to grow to £31.278m by 2028/29, funded primarily by PWLB and council-to-council borrowing
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement will increase from £19.893m (31 March 2025) to £31.278m by 2028/29, an increase of £11.385m over three years. The three-year capital programme totals £109.946m, including major investment via Town Deals. Financing is planned via capital receipts (£27.936m over four years), external contributions (£49.694m), borrowing (£11.385m), and regeneration borrowing (£56.565m). The document states 'significant capital receipts are expected' but gives no timeline or certainty.
findings.matters: The quantum of new borrowing (£67.95m including regeneration) is substantial and contingent on capital receipts that are not quantified. Slippage in receipts or external contributions would require additional PWLB borrowing or repriorisation.
findings.figures: CFR: £19.893m (31.3.25) → £31.278m (by 2028/29). Capital programme £109.946m. Borrowing (standard + regeneration) £67.95m over four years.
findings.quote: The Capital Financing Requirement is set to increase to £31.278m by 2027/28 based on the 3 year Capital Programme for 2026/27 to 2028/29, the Capital Financing Requirement at 31 March 2025 (£19.893m) and the Capital Financing Requirement for capital expenditure during the current financial year and the financial years 2026/27 to 2028/29 (£11.385m).

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Business Rates Reserve drawn down to £1.445m in 2027 to cover collection fund deficit from prior years
findings.detail: The forecast Business Rates reserve balance falls from £2.675m (31 March 2026) to £1.445m (31 March 2027). The document explains this is due to repayment of a deficit relating to 2024/25 and 2025/26. The reserve is explicitly held 'to mitigate against future collection fund losses' and as a contingency for Fair Funding Review variance.
findings.matters: Collection fund deficits in prior years suggest business rates income shortfalls, and the reserve drawdown reduces the council's buffer against further volatility. The reserve is already earmarked for Fair Funding Review risk.
findings.figures: Business Rates Reserve: £2.675m (31.3.26) → £1.445m (31.3.27)
findings.quote: A deficit relating to 2024/25 and 2025/26 will be repayable by the Council in 2026/27 – the reduced forecast balance at 31 March 2027 of the reserve reflects this repayment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation costs of £0.400m in 2026/27 indicate structural uncertainty ahead
findings.detail: The MTFS includes an allowance for costs associated with Local Government Reorganisation of £0.400m in 2026/27, decreasing to £0.200m in 2027/28 and nil in 2028/29. This is not explained further in the document, but signals the council may be subject to restructuring or merger proposals.
findings.matters: Reorganisation costs are a sign of institutional change; if the reorganisation proceeds, transition costs could escalate, and if it does not, the budget benefit of the assumed nil allocation in 2028/29 will not materialise.
findings.quote: A small number of new pressures facing the Council in 2026/27 have also been provided for, these include an allowance for costs associated with Local Government Re-organisation amounting to £0.400m (decreasing to £0.200m in 2027/28 and nil in 2028/29).

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will cut government funding by £0.964m in 2026/27, with only £0.500m pre-funded
findings.detail: The council's redistribution exposure under the Fair Funding Review 2.0 will reduce from £9.360m (2025/26) to £8.396m (2026/27). The council set aside £0.500m in the previous year to prepare, leaving a £0.464m gap to close. The modelling depends on an assumption that the Social Care Grant will be rolled into redistribution; if it is not, the council's share would decrease further.
findings.matters: A £0.964m funding cut is concrete loss of grant, not service demand. If the Social Care Grant assumption fails, the pressure is larger.
findings.quote: Funding received and retained by the Council in 2025/26 that is subject to redistribution under the Fair Funding Review amounts to £9.360m, including the benefits referred to at 2.17, for 2026/27 it is anticipated through comprehensive modelling that this will amount to £8.396m – a reduction in funding of £0.964m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Capital Budget 2026-27 - First Draft Savings Plans - DECEMBER 2025.doc
findings.headline: Largest single saving (£601k, 34% of total) depends on pension fund remaining well-funded.
findings.detail: Staffing savings of £601k described as "Reduction in primary and secondary contributions to reflect improved funding levels". This is not an operational efficiency; it's a discretionary reduction based on pension fund assumptions. If fund deteriorates or contribution rates increase, this saving reverses to become a cost pressure.
findings.matters: Pension obligations are long-term and fixed. If contribution assumptions fail, council faces unexpected cost pressures. Lenders need to understand whether long-term commitments are secure.
findings.figures: £601k pension contribution saving; £638k total staffing related savings (pension savings are 94% of staffing savings)
findings.quote: Pension Contributions 601 Reduction in primary and secondary contributions to reflect improved funding levels

findings.paper_title: Revenue Capital Budget 2026-27 - First Draft Savings Plans - DECEMBER 2025.doc
findings.headline: £109.9m capital programme relies on three large regeneration schemes delivering capital receipts in 2028/29-2031.
findings.detail: York Place: £18.136m spend over 2025/26–2027/28, receipt expected 2028/29. Midway Carpark: £36.350m spend through 2028/29, receipt in 2029/30. Ryecroft: £33.712m spend through 2029/30, receipt in 2030/31. Funding model assumes £12.7m regeneration receipts and £56.6m regeneration borrowing. If receipts are delayed or materially reduced, programme becomes unfunded. Capital Financing Requirement rising to £31.278m by 2028/29.
findings.matters: Large capital schemes carry delivery and market risk. If receipts fail to materialize, council faces either programme cuts, higher borrowing costs, or reserve drawdown. Lenders need confidence these projects will deliver.
findings.figures: £18.136m York Place, £36.350m Midway Carpark, £33.712m Ryecroft, £109.946m total 2026–2029, £12.655m regeneration receipts forecast, £56.565m regeneration borrowing, CFR £31.278m by 2028/29
findings.quote: The Capital Programme for 2026/27 to 2028/29 includes an estimate for the development of York Place, this assumes spend of £18.136m over the period 2025/26 to 2027/28 and a subsequent capital receipt of the same value plus capitalised interest during 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Capital Budget 2026-27 - First Draft Savings Plans - DECEMBER 2025.doc
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will reduce government funding by £0.964m in 2026/27, but settlement not yet confirmed.
findings.detail: Council's government funding (Business Rates and grants subject to redistribution) forecast to drop from £9.360m to £8.396m. This £0.964m reduction has only been partially provided for in the 2025/26 budget (£0.500m set aside). Settlement notification due in December but "estimates are provided regarding likely funding, but it must be stressed that these may be subject to change."
findings.matters: Material uncertainty in government funding affects the council's ability to service debt and deliver services. If settlement is worse than forecast, it requires further budget cuts mid-year.
findings.figures: £9.360m (2025/26) reduces to £8.396m (2026/27) = £0.964m reduction; £0.500m provided; £0.464m gap remains as 2026/27 pressure
findings.quote: Funding received and Business Rates retained by the Council in 2025/26 that are subject to redistribution under the Fair Funding Review amount to £9.360m, for 2026/27 it is anticipated through comprehensive modelling that this will amount to £8.396m – a reduction in funding of £0.964m.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Capital Budget 2026-27 - First Draft Savings Plans - DECEMBER 2025.doc
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer warns significant budget risks mean reserves will need to be called on.
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer's statutory report identifies specific risks that could derail the budget: spending exceeding budget, income falling short (especially capital receipts from major capital schemes), and changes to government funding. Officer explicitly flags that reserves will need to be drawn on if these risks materialize.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess reserve adequacy and budget resilience. Finance directors need to plan for potential drawdowns and ensure reserves are sufficient for the identified risks.
findings.figures: Risks identified: spending overruns, capital receipt shortfalls, government funding changes
findings.quote: In the context of uncertainty regarding Government funding reforms there are significant budget risks that will need to be managed. It will be essential the Council has sufficient reserves to call on if required.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Housing affordability crisis is creating unquantified pressure on homelessness and temporary accommodation services
findings.detail: The document notes that low housing supply relative to demand and the cost-of-living crisis are creating affordability pressures on residents. This is pushing demand for homelessness and temporary accommodation services, which are typically high-cost, unpredictable services. The MTFS does not separately quantify this emerging pressure, and the document acknowledges the risk of dampening council tax income from residents struggling with affordability.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted demand for high-cost services (homelessness, temp accommodation) can create in-year pressure; falling council tax income from households struggling with affordability directly hits a core funding source.
findings.figures: Housing affordability ratio 6.1 (lower than England average 7.7 but indicates pressure); population increase 3.8% but housing supply not kept pace; pressure noted as existing but not separately costed
findings.quote: The resulting affordability gap for residents influenced by the cost of living puts pressure on our homelessness and temporary accommodations services but also has the risk of dampening council tax income.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: 2026/27 budget balanced on £1.752m of identified savings, with £638k being a one-off staffing restructuring
findings.detail: The council has identified £1.752m of savings for 2026/27 to meet the funding gap, but the composition is concerning: £638k is staffing-related (appearing in 2026/27 only, suggesting one-off restructuring); £474k is described as 'Other Financing' without explanation; the remainder is from tax base growth and council tax increases. Delivery of these savings is not certain.
findings.matters: If savings are not realised—particularly the £638k one-off restructuring or the unexplained £474k—the budget will run into deficit in-year, requiring emergency reserves or further cuts.
findings.figures: Savings target: £1.752m for 2026/27; Staffing-related: £638k (2026/27 only); Other Financing: £474k (2026/27 only); Tax base: £308k; Council Tax increase: £179k; Good housekeeping: £66k; Income generation: £87k
findings.quote: To date savings of £1.752m have been identified for 2026/27 enabling a balanced position to be proposed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Collection fund deficit from previous years will be repaid in 2026/27, eroding Business Rates reserve by £1.230m
findings.detail: A collection fund deficit relating to 2024/25 and 2025/26 must be repaid in 2026/27. This causes the Business Rates reserve (which buffers against future collection losses) to fall from a forecast £2.675m at 31 March 2026 to £1.445m at 31 March 2027. This represents a one-time cash cost that reduces financial buffers.
findings.matters: Depletes the council's contingency for business rates volatility or the Fair Funding Review varying from estimates; a smaller reserve means less ability to absorb future shocks.
findings.figures: Business Rates reserve: £2.675m (31.3.26) → £1.445m (31.3.27); repayment reducing the reserve by approximately £1.230m
findings.quote: A deficit relating to 2024/25 and 2025/26 will be repayable by the Council in 2026/27 – the reduced forecast balance at 31 March 2027 of the reserve reflects this repayment.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: £109.946m capital programme over three years requires significant borrowing of £56.565m, dependent on future capital receipts
findings.detail: The council is planning a large regeneration investment programme funded by external contributions (primarily Town Deals), capital receipts, and £56.565m of borrowing. The Capital Financing Requirement will increase to £31.278m by 2027/28. Large capital receipts (£17m) are expected in 2028/29 but only modest receipts in 2026/27 and 2027/28, creating timing risk.
findings.matters: Substantial borrowing increases debt servicing costs and refinancing risk; delayed or reduced capital receipts could require additional borrowing or revenue cuts.
findings.figures: Capital Programme: £109.946m over 3 years; Regeneration Borrowing: £56.565m total; CFR rising to £31.278m by 2027/28; Capital receipts: £5.050m (2026/27), £4.350m (2027/28), £17.006m (2028/29)
findings.quote: These schemes total £109.946m including major investment into the Borough via external funding in terms of the Town Deals Fund for both Newcastle and Kidsgrove and associated projects.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026-2031
findings.headline: Fair Funding Review 2.0 reduces settlement funding by £0.964m in 2026/27 with only partial mitigation in place
findings.detail: The council's settlement funding subject to redistribution under the Fair Funding Review is forecast to fall from £9.360m in 2025/26 to £8.396m in 2026/27. Only £0.500m was set aside in 2025/26 to meet this, leaving a £0.464m gap in 2026/27 that must be addressed through other means.
findings.matters: A material reduction in a core funding source impacts borrowing capacity and financial resilience; the gap must be met by savings or drawdown of reserves.
findings.figures: £9.360m (2025/26) → £8.396m (2026/27), a reduction of £0.964m; £0.500m set aside, leaving £0.464m gap
findings.quote: As part of the 2025/26 budget setting £0.500m was set aside to contribute to this anticipated reduction, as such a gap of £0.464m remains and has been included as a pressure to be addressed for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Pension scheme membership moving into surplus; complex IFRS accounting required revised actuarial report with £1.869m impact
findings.detail: KPMG notes that market conditions mean many councils are finding pension surpluses growing and becoming material, requiring complex accounting under IFRS/SORP. Newcastle-under-Lyme's initial IAS 19 report (25 April 2025) showed variances that exceeded acceptable thresholds; a revised report (23 May 2025) was issued. Corrected misstatements totalling £1.869m were recorded related to asset remeasurement and employer contributions, reflecting the revised actuarial data.
findings.matters: Pension surplus recognition involves complex accounting with high estimation uncertainty. A late actuarial revision forcing corrected misstatements suggests the initial actuary work or council review was inadequate. Lenders care about the materiality and reliability of pension asset/liability positions.
findings.figures: Corrected misstatement - remeasurement gain/loss increase £1.869m; employer contributions increase £257k; benefits adjustment £132k
findings.quote: Also, recent changes to market conditions have meant that more councils are finding themselves moving into surplus in their Local Government Pension Scheme (or surpluses have grown and have become material). The requirements of the accounting standards on recognition of these surplus are complicated and requires actuarial involvement.

findings.headline: Valuation working papers contained formula errors and unused data inputs not caught by management review
findings.detail: On receipt of workings supporting asset valuations, KPMG identified formula errors in key assumptions and relevant data provided by finance (e.g., cashflows) that had not been appropriately applied. This evidenced lack of formal review by management. KPMG recommended formal review of significant valuation workings, particularly those reliant on finance team inputs. Management responded that valuations will continue to be formally reviewed each year.
findings.matters: Management bears ultimate responsibility for valuations in the financial statements despite relying on internal valuers. Unreviewed working papers with formula errors suggest control gaps. This is particularly material given the Castle Car Park (£12m) was valued on investment method during the year.
findings.figures: Issues found in workings for two specific assets; Castle Car Park construction cost £12m, valued at existing use value using investment method
findings.quote: On receipt of the workings to support the valuation of two specific assets, we identified formula errors for key assumptions in the valuation. Similarly, relevant data inputs had been provided by finance (e.g cashflows) which had not been appropriately applied to elements of the workings evidencing a lack of review by management over the valuation workings.

findings.headline: £630k in uncorrected audit misstatements not adjusted in the financial statements
findings.detail: KPMG identified three uncorrected misstatements totalling £630k: £255k York Place investment property (inappropriate revenue capitalisation mixed with capital spend); £885k pension assets (returns variance); and £896k Ryecroft land (should be asset held for sale, not PPE). KPMG notes these have no effect on the audit opinion individually or in aggregate, but formally requested adjustment under ISA 450.
findings.matters: Uncorrected misstatements, however small individually, represent errors in the financial statements. Accumulation across years creates risk. Lenders review audit findings to assess financial statement reliability; uncorrected items suggest either weak controls or disputed valuations.
findings.figures: Total uncorrected misstatements £630k (0.3% of assets, 0.4% of reserves); Investment property error £255k; Pension error £885k; Land reclassification £896k
findings.quote: The aggregated surplus impact of unadjusted audit differences would be £0.2m. In line with ISA 450 we request that you adjust for these items. However, they will have no effect on the opinion in the auditor's report, individually or in aggregate.

findings.headline: Journal entry approval controls inadequate: junior staff can approve entries from seniors, with undocumented review precision
findings.detail: KPMG's detailed ISA 315(R) evaluation of controls found the ledger system permits approval of journals by team members more junior than the poster. Review precision prior to approval is not sufficiently documented to enable audit reliance as a manual control. KPMG could not rely on segregation of duties in journal entry processing, though management considers controls proportionate to risk.
findings.matters: Inadequate journal entry controls create fraud and error risk. This is a core financial reporting control responding to a significant audit risk. Lenders need confidence that material entries are properly reviewed and authorized.
findings.figures: 9 high-risk journal entries identified; no issues found in those tested
findings.quote: Under the requirements of ISA315r, we conduct a detailed evaluation of the design and implementation of controls around journal entries. This identified that the ledger system permits approval of journals by team members that are more junior than the poster.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered only £26.3m of £51.3m planned spend; recurring underspend raises forecasting credibility
findings.detail: The mid-year revised capital budget of £51.3m achieved only £26.3m expenditure (£25.1m under). This follows a prior-year £44m underspend. KPMG notes: 'following multiple years of delayed delivery, there is a risk that the Council loses credibility over its ability to forecast and progress schemes effectively.' Much relates to externally funded projects.
findings.matters: Repeated material underspends suggest either poor forecasting capability or difficulty executing schemes. For lenders, this indicates potential project delivery risk and questions the reliability of capital planning. For finance officers, it damages credibility in budget setting.
findings.figures: Capital budget £51.3m revised; actual spend £26.3m; underspend £25.1m; prior year underspend £44m
findings.quote: Whilst the underspend was much improved on the prior year (£44m underspend in 23-24), following multiple years of delayed delivery, there is a risk that the Council loses credibility over its ability to forecast and progress schemes effectively.

findings.headline: Pension liability decreased by £22.1m but with £885k uncorrected valuation error accumulated over prior years
findings.detail: The council's Local Government Pension Scheme liability fell 13.8% due to actuarial gains from changed assumptions. However, KPMG identified an £885k uncorrected misstatement in pension asset valuation, driven by differences between actual investment returns and the actuary's estimates; this accumulated a prior-year £293k uncorrected misstatement. The actuary's control review lacks precision and documentation sufficient for audit reliance.
findings.matters: Material balance sheet movements driven by estimates create valuation risk, and uncorrected misstatements accumulating over years suggests control gaps. Lenders need confidence in pension liability accuracy given its size relative to council finances.
findings.figures: Pension liability decreased £22.1m (13.8% reduction); uncorrected pension asset misstatement £885k; prior-year carry-forward £293k
findings.quote: Following this update, all variances fell within acceptable threshold. This misstatement is driven by the differences between actual returns and those estimated by the actuary. This resulted in an unadjusted audit difference of £293k in the prior year, accumulating to £885k in 2024-25.

findings.headline: Castle Car Park £12m capital investment now operational and valued using investment method based on income forecasts, introducing new estimation risk
findings.detail: The council completed construction of the Castle Car Park at £12m during 2024/25 and reclassified it from Asset Under Construction to operational land and buildings. It is being valued at existing use value using the investment method, which depends on forecasted rental income and yield assumptions. This introduces new estimation uncertainty as the valuation relies entirely on assumptions about income-generation potential.
findings.matters: Material capital investment now depends on commercial income forecasts; if rental income underperforms assumptions, both valuation and recoverable asset value are at risk; signals council pursuing revenue-generation strategies dependent on market performance.
findings.figures: £12m capital cost; reclassified from AUC to operational; land and buildings balance sheet movement £2.2m (primarily this reclassification)
findings.quote: However, during the year, the Council has completed the construction of the Castle Car Park at a cost of £12m. This will be valued at its existing use value (EUV) using the investment method (based on its income potential).

findings.headline: Valuation working papers for significant assets contained formula errors and lacked formal management review of key assumptions
findings.detail: The auditors identified formula errors in the working papers supporting valuation of two specific assets. Additionally, data inputs provided by finance (e.g. cashflows) were not appropriately applied to elements of calculations, evidencing lack of management review. An absence of formal control reviewing assumptions adopted by valuers was noted, which directly responds to the significant audit risk over land and buildings valuation.
findings.matters: Material asset valuations (land and buildings £43.2m at prior year-end, £37.6m valued at depreciated replacement cost) are unreliable without proper review controls; directly increases risk of misstated balance sheet values.
findings.figures: Land and buildings £43.2m (prior year); £37.6m valued at DRC; investment property portfolio £13.5m (prior year)
findings.quote: On receipt of the workings to support the valuation of two specific assets, we identified formula errors for key assumptions in the valuation. Similarly, relevant data inputs had been provided by finance (e.g cashflows) which had not been appropriately applied to elements of the workings evidencing a lack of review by management over the valuation workings.

findings.headline: Pension asset valuation contained £885k uncorrected misstatement driven by actuary's return assumptions diverging significantly from actual
findings.detail: The council's IAS 19 actuarial valuation required revision from the initial 25 April 2025 report to a revised 23 May 2025 report after variances with actual benefits paid and contributions exceeded acceptable thresholds. The auditors identified a £885k uncorrected misstatement in pension assets, primarily because the actuary's estimated return rate diverged materially from actual administrator returns. This includes a £293k prior year misstatement that was not corrected.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are material to council balance sheet (£137.6m); audit uncertainty about valuation methodology and actuary assumptions indicates control gap; uncorrected misstatements accumulating across years.
findings.figures: £885k uncorrected misstatement in 2024/25 (£293k prior year unadjusted); pension obligation £137.6m (down £22.1m year-on-year); pension assets £176.1m (up £2.6m)
findings.quote: This misstatement is driven by the differences between actual returns and those estimated by the actuary. This includes a £293k prior year misstatement that was uncorrected.

findings.headline: Capital programme underperformance continues: £25.1m underspent against £51.3m revised budget in 2024/25, following £44m underspend in 2023/24
findings.detail: The council began the year with a £59.9m capital programme of which £42.2m was delayed expenditure from 2023/24 when only 21% of budget was spent due to inflationary pressures. After mid-year review, the revised programme totalled £51.295m but actual expenditure reached only £26.3m. The auditors flag this persistent pattern as raising a 'risk that the Council loses credibility over its ability to forecast and progress schemes effectively' and recommend more robust challenge and monitoring with clear communication of slippage.
findings.matters: Persistent capital underspend signals forecasting weakness and delivery risk on council priorities; for lenders, unreliable project forecasting and execution capability poses risk to cashflow and asset deployment.
findings.figures: £59.9m initial programme; £51.295m revised programme; £26.3m actual spend (£25.1m below plan); prior year £44m underspend from 21% budget execution rate
findings.quote: following multiple years of delayed delivery, there is a risk that the Council loses credibility over its ability to forecast and progress schemes effectively

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation will create unquantified budget costs
findings.detail: The council has included a budget pressure for Local Government Reorganisation but explicitly states the cost is unknown. An estimate of £400k has been included for 2026/27 but is provisional. Confirmation of transitional arrangements and timing has not yet been received, creating uncertainty in the MTFS.
findings.matters: Unquantified risk to the MTFS that could worsen the budget gap if costs exceed estimates; timing and magnitude remain uncertain
findings.figures: £400k estimated for 2026/27 (explicitly uncertain)
findings.quote: In addition to the above, a budget pressure in respect of Local Government Reorganisation has been included in the MTFS. It is not yet known how much this will cost, therefore this will be closely monitored and updated.

findings.headline: General Fund reserve of £2.007m is assessed as fully committed to covering identified risks
findings.detail: A preliminary risk assessment indicates that the current General Fund reserve of £2.007m is needed to provide sufficient cover for identified risks. This suggests reserves are already committed and cannot absorb additional pressures without either drawing on other reserves or requiring further savings.
findings.matters: Tight reserve position limits the council's financial flexibility to absorb unexpected pressures; any further deterioration would require immediate savings or borrowing
findings.figures: £2.007m General Fund reserve
findings.quote: A preliminary assessment suggests that the current General Fund reserve of £2.007m will be required to provide sufficient cover for potential risks.

findings.headline: Borrowing costs forecast to escalate significantly in out-years as capital programme matures
findings.detail: Capital financing requirement is estimated to reach £42.490m by 2035/36. Borrowing revenue budget of £0.947m is increasing by £0.058m for 2026/27, with forecast costs spiking to £200k in 2029/30 and £535k in 2030/31, reflecting the growing debt service impact of the capital programme.
findings.matters: Growing debt service obligations will consume increasing amounts of future revenue budgets and reduce financial flexibility, particularly from 2029/30 onwards
findings.figures: Current budget £0.947m; increase £0.058m for 2026/27; £200k additional in 2029/30; £535k additional in 2030/31; total capital requirement £42.490m by 2035/36
findings.quote: The capital financing requirement is estimated to increase to £42.490m by 2035/36 based on the current capital programme and the revenue implications have been reflected in the revised MTFS. It is anticipated that the current borrowing revenue budget of £0.947m will need to be increased by £0.058m to provide for borrowing costs that may be incurred during 2026/27.

findings.headline: Budget gap of £1.777m in 2026/27 with savings proposals not due until December
findings.detail: The MTFS forecasts a budget gap of £1.777m in 2026/27 and £3.069m over the five-year period. Detailed budget proposals including savings and investment plans are scheduled to be presented to Cabinet in December 2025, with final council approval in February 2026, creating a compressed timeline for meaningful scrutiny.
findings.matters: Material budget shortfall requiring significant savings or income generation; tight timeline increases risk of inadequate scrutiny or solutions
findings.quote: The current forecast around financial pressures facing the Council is for a gap in 2026/27 of £1.777m and over the 5-year period of the MTFS, £3.069m.

findings.headline: Fair Funding Review will cut government funding by £0.964m in 2026/27
findings.detail: Funding subject to redistribution under the Fair Funding Review drops from £9.360m (2025/26) to £8.396m (2026/27), a reduction of £0.964m. The council set aside £0.5m in 2025/26 to cushion part of this impact, leaving a £0.464m gap to be addressed in the 2026/27 budget.
findings.matters: Real, measurable loss of government funding that forms half of the overall budget gap and is locked in by central government policy
findings.quote: Funding received and retained by the Council in 2025/26 that is subject to redistribution under the Fair Funding Review amounts to £9.360m, for 2026/27 it is anticipated through comprehensive modelling that this will amount to £8.396m – a reduction in funding of £0.964m.

findings.headline: Medium-term funding gap of £1.777m in 2026/27 with no savings plan presented
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £1.777m gap in 2026/27 and £3.069m over the full five-year MTFS. The report states that work is underway to develop savings proposals to close this gap, but none are presented. Savings proposals are not due to Cabinet until December 2025, leaving a compressed timetable to identify and consult on £1.777m of cuts.
findings.matters: The council has not yet identified how it will balance its budget within a six-month window, and given the minimal reserves and escalating pressures, there is execution risk
findings.quote: The current forecast around financial pressures facing the Council is for a gap in 2026/27 of £1.777m and over the 5-year period of the MTFS, £3.069m.

findings.headline: General Fund reserve of £2.007m at minimum necessary level with no surplus capacity
findings.detail: A risk assessment of reserves concludes that the current General Fund reserve of £2.007m is required just to cover assessed risks. This leaves no discretionary buffer to absorb unexpected expenditure, income shortfalls, or emergencies.
findings.matters: Minimal reserves mean the council cannot self-insure against forecast pressures, making it dependent on external funding or forced service cuts if actual spending exceeds budget
findings.figures: £2.007m General Fund reserve
